explain.say: The appendix is a small, finger-shaped pouch, about 9 centimetres long, hanging off the start of the large intestine in the lower right of the belly. For a long time people thought it was useless.

explain.say: Charles Darwin suggested it was a leftover from ancestors with a much bigger pouch, the caecum, used for digesting tough plant food. Organs left over from ancestors like this are called vestigial.

explain.say: Newer research suggests it may have a job: storing a reserve of helpful gut bacteria, tucked out of the main flow, which can help regrow the gut's bacteria after an upset stomach washes them out.

explain.say: The appendix also contains lots of lymph tissue, which may help train the immune system in the gut. Scientists still debate how important these jobs are, because people live normally without one.

faq.a: Its job is not fully settled. Leading ideas are that it stores helpful gut bacteria as a backup and that its lymph tissue helps the gut's immune system. People can live normally without it.

faq.q: How could the appendix store bacteria?
faq.a: Its narrow, dead-end shape keeps it out of the main stream of the gut. Scientists think a film of helpful bacteria can survive there and recolonise the intestine after illness flushes the gut out.
asks: Tell me about the bacteria safe house

faq.a: A vestigial organ is a body part that seems to have lost most of its original job over evolution, like the tiny tailbone in humans. Darwin thought the appendix was one, though it may still have some uses.
asks: Tell me about the leftover pouch

faq.a: It hangs off the caecum, the first part of the large intestine, usually in the lower right part of the belly.
asks: Which side is the appendix on?

faq.q: Do other animals have an appendix?
faq.a: Yes. An appendix has appeared independently in many mammals, including rabbits, some rodents and many primates, which suggests it can be useful.

facts: The human appendix is usually about 8 to 10 centimetres long.
Charles Darwin proposed in 1871 that the appendix was a vestigial remnant of a larger caecum.
An appendix has evolved independently many times in mammals.
